summary.text: Writing \(n=p^2c\), the binomial theorem shows that every term of \((k+pc)^p-k^p\) is divisible by \(p^2c\), so \(n/p=pc\) is a period, while shifting by \(n\) is always a period. For any positive period \(T\), evaluation at \(0\) and \(1\), together with the prime divisibility of the intermediate binomial coefficients, gives \(n\mid T^p\) and \(n\mid pT(1+TK)\) for some \(K\); since \(1+TK\) is coprime to \(n\), this forces \(n\mid pT\), from which \(n/p\mid T\) when \(p^2\mid n\), and \(n\mid T\) otherwise.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_{p,n}=\left\{T\in\mathbb N: T>0\text{ and }(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n\text{ for every }k\in\mathbb N\right\}.
\]
For positive \(n\), the number \(a_p(n)\) is the least element of this set. We prove that this least element is
\[
\begin{cases}
n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\]
Throughout, \(p\) is prime and \(n>0\). In particular, \(p\ge 2\).

## 1. The proposed numbers really are periods

First, \(n\) itself is always a period. Indeed,
\[
k+n\equiv k\pmod n,
\]
and raising congruent integers to the \(p\)-th power preserves congruence. Thus
\[
(k+n)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\). Since \(n>0\), this proves \(n\in S_{p,n}\), so in particular the set of positive periods is nonempty.

Now suppose that \(p^2\mid n\). Write
\[
n=p^2c
\]
for some \(c\in\mathbb N\). Since \(n>0\), also \(c>0\). As \(p>0\),
\[
\frac np=pc.
\]
We claim that \(pc\) is a period modulo \(p^2c\). By the binomial theorem,
\[
(k+pc)^p-k^p
 =\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\binom pi k^i(pc)^{p-i}.
\]
Every summand on the right is divisible by \(p^2c\). There are two cases.

* If \(i=p-1\), then \(p-i=1\) and \(\binom p{p-1}=p\), so the summand is
  \[
  k^{p-1}(pc)p=p^2c\,k^{p-1}.
  \]

* If \(i\le p-2\), then \(p-i\ge2\), and hence
  \[
  (pc)^{p-i}=p^2c\bigl(c(pc)^{p-i-2}\bigr).
  \]
  Thus this summand is again divisible by \(p^2c\).

Consequently the entire difference is divisible by \(p^2c=n\), and therefore
\[
(k+pc)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\). Hence \(n/p=pc\in S_{p,n}\).

It remains to prove that no smaller positive period can occur.

## 2. Two divisibility consequences of an arbitrary period

Let \(T\in S_{p,n}\). Thus \(T>0\) and
\[
(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb N.
\]
Taking \(k=0\), and using \(p>0\), gives
\[
T^p\equiv0^p=0\pmod n.
\]
Therefore
\[
 n\mid T^p. \tag{1}
\]

Taking \(k=1\) gives
\[
(1+T)^p\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
 n\mid (1+T)^p-1. \tag{2}
\]
We next extract from (1) and (2) the more useful conclusion
\[
 n\mid pT. \tag{3}
\]

For this purpose, we first establish the required form of the binomial expansion. For every integer \(j\) with \(1\le j\le p-1\), primality of \(p\) implies
\[
p\mid\binom pj.
\]
For completeness, one can see this from
\[
j\binom pj=p\binom{p-1}{j-1}.
\]
The right side is divisible by \(p\), while \(p\nmid j\) because \(0<j<p\); Euclid's lemma therefore gives \(p\mid\binom pj\).

Expanding \((1+T)^p\), separating the terms of degrees \(0,1,p\), and using this divisibility for all the intermediate coefficients, we can write
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1+T)^p
 &=1+pT+\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}\binom pjT^j+T^p\\
 &=1+pT+pT^2K+T^p\\
 &=1+pT(1+TK)+T^p                                      \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
for some nonnegative integer \(K\). Explicitly, when \(p>2\) one may take
\[
K=\sum_{j=2}^{p-1}\frac1p\binom pjT^{j-2},
\]
and when the intermediate sum is empty, as for \(p=2\), take \(K=0\).

Combining (2) with (4), we obtain
\[
n\mid pT(1+TK)+T^p.
\]
Together with (1), subtraction yields
\[
n\mid pT(1+TK).                                      \tag{5}
\]

We claim that
\[
\gcd(n,1+TK)=1.                                       \tag{6}
\]
Suppose otherwise. Then some prime \(q\) divides both \(n\) and \(1+TK\). Since \(q\mid n\) and \(n\mid T^p\) by (1), we have \(q\mid T^p\). A prime dividing a power divides its base, so \(q\mid T\). Hence \(q\mid TK\). But \(q\mid1+TK\) as well, and subtracting \(TK\) would give \(q\mid1\), an impossibility. Thus no prime divides both numbers, proving (6).

Since \(n\) is coprime to \(1+TK\), the factor \(1+TK\) can be canceled from (5): if a number \(n\) is coprime to \(A\) and divides \(xA\), then it divides \(x\). We conclude that
\[
 n\mid pT,                                             \tag{7}
\]
as asserted.

Thus every positive period \(T\) satisfies both
\[
n\mid T^p\qquad\text{and}\qquad n\mid pT.           \tag{8}
\]

## 3. Lower bound when \(p^2\mid n\)

Assume first that \(p^2\mid n\). In particular, \(p\mid n\). Put
\[
m=\frac np,
\]
so that \(n=mp\). By (7), \(mp=n\mid pT\). Since \(p>0\), cancellation of \(p\) gives
\[
m\mid T.
\]
As \(T>0\), divisibility implies
\[
\frac np=m\le T.                                      \tag{9}
\]
We already proved in Section 1 that \(n/p\) itself is a positive period. Equation (9) shows that every positive period is at least \(n/p\). Therefore the least positive period is exactly
\[
a_p(n)=\frac np
\]
when \(p^2\mid n\).

## 4. Lower bound when \(p^2\nmid n\)

Now assume
\[
p^2\nmid n.
\]
We prove from (8) that \(n\mid T\). There are two subcases.

### Subcase 4.1: \(p\nmid n\)

Because \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(n\), we have \(\gcd(n,p)=1\). From \(n\mid pT\), cancellation of the coprime factor \(p\) gives
\[
n\mid T.
\]

### Subcase 4.2: \(p\mid n\)

Let
\[
m=\frac np,
\]
so \(n=mp\). From \(n\mid pT\), we have \(mp\mid pT\), and cancellation of the positive factor \(p\) gives
\[
m\mid T.                                             \tag{10}
\]
Also, since \(p\mid n\) and \(n\mid T^p\), we have \(p\mid T^p\). Primality of \(p\) then gives
\[
p\mid T.                                             \tag{11}
\]
Moreover, \(m\) and \(p\) are coprime. Indeed, if \(p\mid m\), then
\[
p^2\mid mp=n,
\]
contrary to the present assumption. Since \(p\) is prime, \(p\nmid m\) is exactly the assertion \(\gcd(m,p)=1\).

It follows from (10), (11), and coprimality that the product \(mp\) divides \(T\). Since \(mp=n\), this is
\[
n\mid T.
\]

Thus in either subcase, every positive period \(T\) is divisible by \(n\), and consequently
\[
n\le T.                                              \tag{12}
\]
Section 1 showed that \(n\) itself is a positive period. Therefore (12) proves that the least positive period is exactly
\[
a_p(n)=n
\]
when \(p^2\nmid n\).

Combining the two cases yields
\[
\boxed{
 a_p(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
 n,&p^2\nmid n.
 \end{cases}}
\]
This is the claimed formula.
